etymologies.etymologyHTML: From commerce +‎ -ial. From French commercial (“of, or pertaining to commerce”), from Late Latin commercialis, from Latin commercium.

definitions.definition: An advertisement in a common media format, usually radio or television.
(finance) A commercial trader, as opposed to an individual speculator.

quote.citation: 1875, George Worsley, Advice to the Young!, page 32:
quote.text: I have more than once had to lend a commercial money to pay his fare home; as he had played shell-out and lost the lot.
Five persons went to the house after the milkman was gone, and that there Arab party was safe inside, — three of them was commercials, that I know, because afterwards they came to me.

quote.citation: 1972, Alfred Eustace Parker, The Berkeley Police Story, page 133:
quote.text: Tom said that homosexuals hate “commercials,” male prostitutes, and if the homosexual was drunk and angry, he might have committed murder.

quote.citation: 1987, Paul William Mathews, Male Prostitution: Two Monographs, page 39:
quote.text: With the commercials there is no intensity of feeling and no later animosity; there is emotional and sexual fakery, but no prolonged post-sexual bargaining.  […]  Paradoxically these boys dissociate themselves from the commercials, yet engage in prostitution only when they require the money.

quote.citation: 1900, Charles W[addell] Chesnutt, chapter I, in The House Behind the Cedars, Boston, Mass.; New York, N.Y.: Houghton, Mifflin and Company […], →OCLC:
quote.text: A two minutes' walk brought Warwick--the name he had registered under, and as we shall call him--to the market-house, the central feature of Patesville, from both the commercial and the picturesque points of view.

definitions.definition: (aviation) Designating an airport that serves passenger and/or cargo flights.
